rationales.A: The passage joins work, goods, and Protestant faith in one argument — trade and religion served the same rivalry with Spain.
rationales.B: The passage leads with work for the poor and goods from abroad; profit is at the heart of the argument, not an afterthought.
rationales.C: Hakluyt appealed to investors and settlers through companies, not to the crown to rule the colonies itself.
rationales.D: Hakluyt argued for planting settlements and trading, not for conquering an empire of silver mines as Spain had done.
rationales.general:
1. Notice the joining. One sentence carries work, timber, and Protestant faith together — Hakluyt does not separate them.
2. Ask what ties them. Background: Catholic Spain was England's great rival, and every English gain was also a blow against Spain.
3. Ask what the colony would do. Grow goods, employ the poor, and plant Protestant settlers on the edge of a Catholic empire.
4. Name the double purpose. English colonization was business and rivalry at once.
Remember: when a source mixes money and faith, it is describing one rivalry in two languages.

stimulus.source_note: Original secondary passage written for this question, paraphrasing Richard Hakluyt's arguments for English colonization in the 1580s.
stimulus.text: In the 1580s Richard Hakluyt argued that England should plant colonies in America. He said the colonies would give work to England's idle poor, provide timber and other goods that England bought from foreign rivals, and spread the Protestant faith against Catholic Spain.
